title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired evaluation to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces the incidence of security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent-to-configuration pipeline. Using a Dockerized FRRouting-style emulator, two deterministic validators (containerized Batfish and a Python graph-based static reachability analyzer), and a matched sample of N=300 intents (150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants), we compared single-pass LLM generation (baseline) to an LLM+verifier GVR pipeline implemented with gpt-5-mini under a preregistered protocol (study cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). The run completed the planned 600 episodes, consuming 300 model calls (shared-initial-generation semantics: one LLM call per pair) and zero failed episodes. The confirmatory outcome was degenerate: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (contingency n11=300, n10=n01=n00=0). Paired risk-difference = 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, 95% bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Importantly, the GVR repair step was never exercised: verifier checks did not trigger any repair attempts across the dataset, so guarded episodes observed identical initial candidates to baseline. We report the preregistration, execution and analysis artifacts, and interpret the null as a consequence of task/design selection (perfect baseline compliance under the chosen safety predicate) rather than general evidence that verifiers are unnecessary. We close with recommendations for adversarially stronger benchmarks and alternative experimental contracts that would better stress-test verifier-in-the-loop interventions.

sections.introduction: Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models (LLMs) promises operational efficiency but raises safety concerns: generated configurations can introduce security-relevant errors (unauthorized reachability, policy violations, or availability regressions). Prior system and survey work therefore advocates integrating execution-capable validators or closed-loop repair (generate–verify–repair, GVR) to reduce such risks. We ask a focused, preregistered research question: Does embedding a formal reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent-to-configuration pipeline under a deterministic paired evaluation? Our confirmatory contributions are (1) a machine-readable preregistration (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) specifying a paired N=300 design and prespecified analyses; (2) a deterministic Dockerized execution using FRRouting-style images and two deterministic validators; and (3) full execution and analysis artifacts showing that, on the chosen task set and model (gpt-5-mini), baseline single-pass generation already satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate for every tested intent, so the guarded GVR pipeline produced no measurable improvement.
sections.related_work: Two bodies of prior work motivate our design. First, GVR and execution-guided iterative-repair architectures have been shown to improve correctness on code and infrastructure-as-code benchmarks when paired with robust verifiers or execution oracles; these system-level reports and case studies motivate verifier-in-the-loop designs. Second, surveys and NetOps studies show persistent LLM risks—hallucination, overconfidence, and domain mismatch—that motivate validators, constrained generation, and human oversight. However, the literature also documents heterogeneity in reported gains across tasks, models, and verifier strength, and identifies a shortage of execution-validated NetOps benchmarks that systematically stress security-relevant failure modes. Our study targets that evidence gap by preregistering a paired verification experiment that measures forbidden reachability as an operational safety predicate.
sections.methodology: Design and preregistration: We preregistered a deterministic paired experiment (study id cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in proportion of intents yielding forbidden reachability). The prespecified confirmatory test is an exact McNemar-style paired test (alpha=0.05) with bootstrap CIs (1,000 planned resamples; 10,000 used in final analysis). Sampling and tasks: fixed matched sample N=300 (150 benign seeds each paired with one programmatic adversarial variant); deterministic duplicate and fuzzy-deduplication checks applied pre-execution per the preregistration. Intervention and baseline: for each intent pair we executed (A) baseline: single-pass LLM generation (one call to gpt-5-mini) and (B) guarded: LLM initial generation + verifier check + up to one LLM repair attempt (GVR loop). The preregistered GVR repair policy invoked a repair attempt only when the verifier returned a forbidden-reachability violation; at most one repair LLM call was allowed per pair. Shared-initial-generation semantics: the contract used 'shared_initial_candidate' generation_semantics (the same initial LLM candidate was used for both baseline and guarded playback), producing one model call per pair. Validators and environment: experiments ran deterministically in Docker compositions with FRRouting-style router images. Two validators executed deterministically: (i) a containerized Batfish instance as an execution-capable reachability oracle and (ii) a lightweight Python graph-based static reachability analyzer. Validator provenance and deterministic traces are recorded in the evidence bundle: validator identifiers and per-episode validator traces (validator_id field 'deterministic_netops_validator_v5', validator_version '5.0') appear in the scoring and response artifacts. Outcome and missingness: 'success' denotes absence of forbidden reachability as reported by the validators. Prespecified missingness and sensitivity rules treated technical failures separately and are archived in the execution manifest. Reproducibility: preregistration, execution manifest, raw model-call logs, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived and referenced in the evidence bundle.
sections.results: Execution accounting: the run completed all planned episodes (600 episodes = 300 pairs × 2 conditions) and consumed 300 model calls (model_calls_used = 300; maximum_model_calls allowed = 600 under the contract). There were zero failed episodes and no unscorable episodes. Primary confirmatory outcome: complete_pair_count = 300; baseline_success_count = 300; guarded_success_count = 300. The paired contingency table is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] computed from 10,000 resamples (bootstrap seed = 1729). Repair-activity provenance and counts: under the preregistered GVR logic a repair attempt would be issued only when a validator reported a forbidden-reachability violation. Across the full run the verifier never reported forbidden reachability for any initial candidate, and consequently no repair prompts were generated and no repair calls were applied. Evidence for this behavior is in the episode-level validator traces and scoring artifacts (per-episode validator_trace entries show repair_applied = false and repair_prompt_sha256 = null for representative episodes). Model-call accounting: the shared-initial-generation design produced a single LLM call per intent pair (stage_counts in the execution manifest record 'shared_initial_generation' = 300), hence median model-call overhead introduced by the guarded condition is zero for this execution contract. Verifier agreement and secondary estimates: recorded validator outputs showed no disagreements for these episodes under the chosen validators; contamination checks produced no flagged items in analysis/contamination_summary.csv. Representative per-intent scoring and validator-trace artifacts and the full analysis CSVs are archived in the evidence bundle.
sections.discussion: Interpretation of the null: the confirmatory null is degenerate because there were zero discordant pairs (no cases in which baseline produced forbidden reachability while guarded prevented it). In such a dataset McNemar-style inference is uninformative about the practical efficacy of GVR when a nontrivial baseline violation rate exists; our preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction. The observed perfect baseline compliance implies the GVR repair path was never exercised, so this experiment cannot adjudicate whether repairs would rescue violating outputs in genuinely failure-prone settings. Design implications: (1) the shared_initial_generation contract—chosen and frozen in the preregistration—meant baseline and guarded playback used the same initial candidate; this reduces model-call budget usage but also reduces the number of independent LLM generations that could produce discordant erroneous outputs. (2) Because no verifier-detected violations occurred, the GVR loop did not invoke repairs; thus the experiment measured whether verifier insertion changes observed compliance when baseline generation already meets the safety predicate, not whether verifier-guided repair can correct genuine violations. Recommendations: future evaluations aiming to stress-test verifier-in-the-loop efficacy should (a) adopt harder adversarial intent generators, (b) consider independent-condition generation (independent LLM draws per condition) or larger repair budgets to exercise repair paths more often, and (c) evaluate multiple LLMs and stronger oracles to probe conditions under which verifier feedback produces measurable security gains. Reproducibility notes: key artifacts supporting the above claims—execution/execution_manifest.json, execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/contamination_summary.csv, and representative per-episode scoring traces—are archived in the manuscript evidence bundle.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered, deterministic paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent-to-configuration generation using gpt-5-mini over 300 matched intents. The confirmatory outcome was a degenerate null: both baseline and guarded conditions passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11=300). Crucially, the verifier never reported violations and the GVR repair step was never executed under the chosen task generation and execution contract. This result emphasizes that benchmark difficulty and experimental contract design (shared vs independent generation, adversarial potency, repair budget, verifier strength) materially determine whether verifier-in-the-loop architectures can demonstrate benefits. We therefore recommend more adversarial, production-representative workloads and experimental contracts that ensure the repair path is exercised before drawing broad conclusions about verifier efficacy in NetOps security.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11=300, n10=n01=n00=0) render the paired McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better stress the repair path.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.

Contamination risk: deterministic duplicate and fuzzy-deduplication checks were applied prior to execution and analysis/contamination_summary.csv reports no flagged items; residual training-data overlap with hosted LLMs cannot be entirely excluded and is treated in archived sensitivity analyses.
